summary: For ages 6–7, teach that the equals sign means 'is the same value as' / 'balances' — a statement of balance between two expressions, not an instruction to 'work out the answer'. Deliberately vary equation form (answer on the left like 8 = 5+3, operations on both sides like 5+2 = 6+1, bare identity like 8 = 8) and prioritise judging true/false and relational reasoning (compensation) over always computing both sides. A physical or on-screen balance model anchors equality as equilibrium rather than a finish line.
misconceptions: Reading '=' as 'work out the answer' / 'the total goes here' (operator misconception) — so 8 = 5+3 looks 'backwards' or wrong.
Rejecting bare identities like 8 = 8 as 'not a sum' or incomplete.
In a+b = c+□, writing the running total of the left side into the box (e.g. 8+4 = 12+□ → box = 12 or 12+? = to next), the classic Falkner/Carpenter error.
Believing there can only be one number after the '='.
Thinking both sides must LOOK identical rather than share a value.

activities.title: Balance beam: build both sides and watch it level
steps: Set an expression on the left pan and another on the right (for example 5+2 on the left, 6+1 on the right) using identical cubes on a physical pan balance (5 cubes and 2 cubes on one side, 6 cubes and 1 cube on the other), or number/operation tiles on an on-screen balance that weighs each side by its value.
Predict whether the beam will tip or settle level, and say why, before releasing it.
Watch whether the beam tips or settles level: with identical cubes (or an on-screen balance that weighs by value), it sits level only when both sides share the same value.
Try a case where the sides look different but balance: put 8 on the left and 5+3 on the right and observe that the beam still sits level.
Try a missing-number challenge: add to one pan to level the beam, e.g. make 8+3 balance 9+□ (the blank is 2, since both sides then make 11).
activities.insight: The equals sign is the pivot/balance point: two sides are equal when they share the same value, regardless of how each side looks or which side 'the answer' is on. '=' is not a direction to compute leftward.

activities.title: True or false across varied forms
steps: Judge whether each sentence is true or false and say how you decided: 6 = 6; 7 = 8 − 1; 5 + 2 = 2 + 5; 4 + 1 = 5 + 2.
For 5 + 2 = 6 + 1, decide true or false WITHOUT fully computing both sides, using compensation (one more on one side, one less on the other).
Sort a set of equation cards into 'balanced / true' and 'not balanced / false' piles.
Fill a missing number to make the sentence true: 8 = □ + 3 (blank is 5); 8 + 3 = 9 + □ (blank is 2); □ = 7 − 5 (blank is 2).
activities.insight: A number sentence is true when both sides have the same value, in any layout — identity, answer-left, or operations on both sides — and relational reasoning can decide this without always calculating.

activities.title: Static balance picture to anchor 'the same as'
steps: Look at a level balance with an expression on each pan (e.g. 8 on one side, 5+3 on the other).
Tap or point to each side to reveal its value.
Say why the balance stays level: 'both sides are 8, so they balance — that is what = means'.
activities.insight: Both sides of a true equation share one value even when they look different; a level balance pictures this meaning of '='.

activities.title: Talk it through: why is this true?
steps: Answer a partner's or tutor's questions about varied-form equations: 'Is 8 = 5 + 3 true? How do you know?'
Explain why 8 = 8 counts as a true number sentence.
Explain whether 5 + 2 = 6 + 1 is true and how you can tell without adding both sides fully.
Read the '=' sign aloud in words and make a true number sentence with 8 on its own on one side.
activities.insight: Articulating why a sentence balances makes a child's reading of '=' explicit and lets 'answer-comes-next' thinking be noticed and corrected.

checkQuestion: True or false: 5 + 2 = 4 + 3? And true or false: 8 = 8? Tell me how you decided each one.
checkAnswer: Both are TRUE. 5 + 2 = 4 + 3 because both sides have the value 7; 8 = 8 because both sides are the same value. Reason: '=' means 'is the same value as' / both sides balance — it is not an instruction to write an answer.
